ad-or-info.note: Students sort mock media by the creator's purpose and name the persuasion clue, core ELAR author's-purpose work that also builds the grades 3–5 media-spin strand of digital citizenship.

after-the-rumor.note: Staff trace a viral AI-edited photo rumor to root causes, preparing to teach students to check source and context and respond as upstanders instead of forwarding harmful content.

ai-critic-tank.note: Teachers design a community solution by hand, then weigh AI critiques and write an honest disclosure, modeling the design process and ethical crediting students practice in Technology Applications.

ai-ethics-case-court.note: Educators argue both sides of AI uses such as essay scoring and device monitoring, preparing to teach the ethics and privacy substrands of digital citizenship.

ai-guidance-from-values.note: Teams draft campus AI guidance on disclosure and privacy, the expectations students meet in the digital citizenship ethics-and-laws and privacy-and-security substrands.

ai-study-buddy-contract.note: Students decide which AI uses build or replace their learning, set a SMART goal, and log honest AI use, practicing deliberate tool choice and academic integrity.

algorithm-autopsy.note: Students explain how a recommender predicts and ranks content, quote a product memo in seminar, and design a healthier feed with measurable rules and trade-offs.

ask-two.note: Children check a robot helper's claims in a book, by observing, or with a grown-up, early inquiry and scientific observation that shows sure-sounding answers can be wrong.

bias-detectives.note: Teachers design a fair paired-prompt test that changes one variable and repeats runs, preparing students to investigate AI bias with science practices.

bias-in-the-machine.note: Students read mock AI outputs through perspective lenses, quote words that reveal an assumption, and explain how training-data patterns produce stereotypes.

co-creation-not-substitution.note: Teachers write assignment-level AI-use statements and a student disclosure template, preparing students to credit AI help honestly while keeping creative ownership.

community-problem-pitch.note: Students break down a real school problem, gather evidence, then keep, verify, or reject AI critiques before prototyping and pitching a solution.

credit-where-its-due.note: Students write credit lines and AI Help Notes for work they used, the grades 3–5 intellectual property and citing expectations in digital citizenship and ELAR research.

dashboard-critical-read.note: Leaders spot truncated axes, small samples, and proxy metrics, then redraw a chart honestly, the same data-representation and privacy skills they want students to apply.

data-trail-audit.note: Students decode a mock privacy policy, quote the exact wording on collection and sharing, and trace data to brokers, core privacy-and-security work in digital citizenship.

deepfake-election-desk.note: Student newsroom teams verify election media through origin, corroboration, and context, then write an editor's memo separating what was checked from what remains unknown.

deepfake-principal-tabletop.note: Leaders verify a fake principal audio clip by provenance and corroboration rather than detectors, preparing to build the source-reliability habits students need.

did-the-ai-help.note: Educators plan a fair, blind-scored comparison of an AI-supported task, so tool choices in class rest on evidence of student learning.

digital-footprint-trail.note: Students combine a fictional classmate's posts to see what they reveal, then rewrite risky or hurtful ones, the grades 3–5 digital footprint and personal information expectations.

disclose-it.note: Students apply course AI policies to scenarios, then write a specific disclosure and process log and revise it after peer feedback.

does-this-need-a-screen.note: Teachers sort tasks by whether a screen adds evidence of learning, preparing to model purposeful tool choice for students.

evidence-before-tools.note: Teachers rebuild a tool-heavy research lesson from the evidence backward, so students compare sources and justify every tool, including AI, against what it shows.

explain-it-to-grandma.note: Educators explain how chatbots predict text in plain, accurate language, preparing students to explain AI concepts to others with an honest limitation.

family-ai-night-design.note: Campus teams design family stations on how chatbots work, AI-generated images, and app privacy, extending student AI and privacy learning into homes.

five-question-rollout-check.note: Leaders test an AI platform rollout against five questions, including a student's screen-reader barrier, so tool adoption serves every student's learning.

four-lens-app-review.note: Coaches score apps on privacy, accessibility, and AI transparency and verify vendor claims laterally, habits students need for privacy and source reliability.

garbage-in-garbage-out.note: Students write, test, and revise precise step-by-step instructions, then upgrade vague AI prompts, practicing computational thinking and procedural writing.

glass-box-checklist.note: Teams turn vague vendor claims into answerable questions about data and limits, preparing students to ask what apps do with their information.

hallucination-hunt.note: Students trace each claim in an AI research brief to its source, catch fabricated and distorted citations, and revise the brief, core ELAR inquiry and research.

headlines-from-year-three.note: Leadership teams run a pre-mortem on an AI initiative and set guardrails, so tool adoption is judged by what changes for students.

human-ai-studio.note: Students draft flash fiction or a design concept, log every AI suggestion they keep, change, or reject, and disclose AI's role honestly.

human-language-model.note: Educators build a next-word frequency table by hand and watch it hallucinate, a classroom-ready model of how generative AI predicts from patterns.

hype-check-showcase.note: Teachers test tool claims and synthetic media at stations, preparing students to choose tools for learning and check media by source and context.

journal-club-by-design.note: Coaches check a practice article's claims and evidence, then plan teacher learning on pausing before sharing, a digital citizenship habit for students.

kind-by-design.note: Teachers rewrite sharp messages to be kind and clear and co-create norms, preparing to teach digital etiquette and respectful online communication.

kind-clicks.note: Children sort kind and unkind online messages, rewrite unkind ones, and rehearse telling a trusted grown-up, the K–2 social-interactions strand of digital citizenship.

lateral-reading-relay.note: Teachers use SIFT to verify claims, including an AI summary, preparing students to judge source reliability and show verification evidence.

look-fors-for-learning.note: Leaders revise walkthrough rubrics to capture student reasoning and verification of AI output, rather than device use alone.

looking-for-the-checking.note: A PLC reads student Dust Bowl notes for evidence of real checking, then plans instruction on verifying AI claims against independent sources.

my-digital-safety-plan.note: Students audit their own security habits and write a plan with passphrases, two-step login, and privacy settings, the privacy, safety, and security substrand.

never-paste-this.note: Data teams de-identify student notes before any AI use, modeling the personal-information protection students learn in digital citizenship.

news-from-the-future-circle.note: Children name helpful and tricky sides of pretend AI helpers, including that helpers can be wrong and shouldn't get private information.

next-word-by-hand.note: Students tally which word follows which and generate sentences by chance draws, seeing how prediction from patterns can produce a confident false fact.

password-power.note: Students rank passwords, build practice passphrases, and decide who may know a password, core grades 3–5 privacy, safety, and security skills.

personalization-with-guardrails.note: Teachers verify an AI-leveled text and match supports like text-to-speech to learners, so students reach the same grade-level reading target.

phish-tank-irl.note: Students sort realistic messages as safe, scam, or check another way and name red flags that still work, the phishing and security part of digital citizenship.

photo-detective.note: Students investigate cropped, edited, and AI-made photos by checking other coverage, reading images and captions as multimodal texts with a purpose.

primary-source-vs-ai-summary.note: Students compare an AI summary with a primary-source letter, cite paragraphs for each distortion, and write a faithful summary, core social studies source skills.

private-or-share.note: Children sort information into keep private, ask a grown-up, or OK to share and rehearse refusing a chatbot's request, the K–2 personal-information expectation.

real-fake-or-generated.note: Students see visual clues fail and revise verdicts by checking who posted media first, then plan a safe response to a cloned-voice request.

real-pretend-or-changed.note: Children tell real, pretend-on-purpose, and changed or computer-made pictures apart and give a clue, early media literacy about genre and trustworthiness.

real-remixed-or-made-up.note: Teachers label authentic, out-of-context, cheapfake, and synthetic media by provenance, then plan a student version that requires a verification move.

remix-rights.note: Students decide which remixes need credit, permission, or a fair-use argument and write TASL credit lines, the intellectual property core of digital citizenship.

ripple-out-futures-wheel.note: Educators map ripple effects of a near-future AI headline and backcast actions, preparing students to think creatively about technology's consequences.

robot-guesses.note: Children train a pretend robot with example cards, watch it misclassify, and fix it with more varied examples, an early model of how AI learns patterns.

screen-time-green-time.note: Children observe and record how their bodies feel after screen stillness versus movement, then plan a balanced mix of screen and green time.

seminar-on-a-machines-answer.note: Teachers run a Socratic seminar on a chatbot transcript, preparing students to question AI answers and see that agreement is not evidence.

shallow-answers-coaching-cycle.note: Coaches co-plan a lesson that trades question volume for claims backed by class data and reasoning, then measure the change in student work.

signal-to-headline-lab.note: Students write a future news headline, lede, and evidence line, then fact-check a peer's draft for clickbait and invented numbers and revise.

student-voice-policy-makers.note: Students gather stakeholder evidence, draft a technology policy proposal that passes the five-question check, and defend it before a mock board.

study-coach-with-guardrails.note: Students write custom instructions for an AI study coach, stress-test them, and judge with a before-and-after check whether the tool improved learning.

team-tech-choices.note: Teams match project tasks to tools, or no tool, and explain what each choice shows they learned, the tool-selection focus of practical technology concepts.

the-feed-game.note: Students act as a rule-following recommendation algorithm, track topic counts across rounds, and test a rule change against their prediction.

the-prompt-ladder.note: Teachers predict how each added prompt detail changes AI output, preparing to teach students that a prompt is context for prediction and still needs checking.

two-drafts-of-feedback.note: Coaches trace AI-drafted feedback against a transcript and sort observation AI uses by consent and privacy, modeling data protection students also learn.

vendor-claims-vs-evidence.note: Leaders trace a product's marketing claim to its study and flag terms that let student work train AI, the claim-checking and privacy habits students need.

verify-the-bot-workshop.note: Teachers split AI science answers into claims and check each against two independent sources, preparing students to keep a claim ledger in class.

what-do-my-apps-know.note: Teachers audit the privacy policies of tools they use and plan a student lesson on asking what an app knows, the privacy-and-security substrand.

who-gets-left-out-map.note: Teams walk a homework-and-AI-tutor plan through family profiles to find access barriers, so every student can use the tools a lesson requires.

who-made-this.note: Children name who made a piece of media and why, to teach, sell, entertain, or inform, early ELAR author's-purpose work that includes honesty about AI help.

who-owns-the-output.note: Students argue both sides of AI training on artists' work and co-write a credit rule, reasoning about intellectual property in the ethics-and-laws substrand.

whose-story-is-missing.note: Teachers audit AI-generated materials for who is missing or stereotyped, preparing students to question an output's frame of reference and add missing perspectives.
